[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 0.9 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"dcf74b","wall_time_seconds":0.7088613,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":9092,"output":"research-lsatlab-advanced-conditionals.md\\r\\n# Advanced conditional applications\\r\\n\\r\\nSource: [Conditional Logic (adv)](https://app.lsatlab.com/video-library/?videoid=32838), Patrick Tyrrell, 2026-07-15. Parent verified Vimeo 1210390172, duration 93:06.76. Read all 1,441 automatic-caption cues chronologically through 93:03.914. Audio and slides unverified; prompts not copied.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Time | Teaching and training |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| 00:05–05:58 | Distinguishes explicit conditional rules from broad conditional reasoning; locates application families. |\\r\\n| 05:58–28:44 | Parallel-flaw warm-up; independent attempt, private guesses, student explanations, corrections. Reviews invalid moves, abstraction, quantifier matching and overlap. |\\r\\n| 28:48–52:30 | MBT: preserve qualifying details, distinguish obligation from action, avoid inverse reasoning. Discusses unusual contextual biconditional interpretation. |\\r\\n| 52:36–74:03 | SA: isolate conclusion, orient rule by contraposition, identify missing trigger facts. A counterexample to a universal requirement can suffice; semantic matches exceed keyword matches. |\\r\\n| 74:15–79:45 | Principle application: eligible conclusions, compound contraposition, scope and added-claim elimination. |\\r\\n| 79:51–93:03 | Harder MBT: separate certainty from probability, test answer triggers, follow chains without diagramming everything. |\\r\\n\\r\\nPrerequisites: translation, contraposition, AND/OR, quantifiers and question-type methods. New emphasis: strategic transfer and efficiency. Familiar questions are vetoed; harder items follow discussion. No independent mastery rubric observed. Contextual biconditional claims need editorial review; teacher heuristics are not universal logical rules.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original LSAT U examples, not provider material\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Qualifying details:** A grant above $2,000 awarded to a new applicant requires committee review. Keep amount and applicant status together when translating. An experienced applicant\'s award cannot be classified from that rule alone.\\r\\n- **Obligation versus action:** A damaged machine must be inspected. An undamaged machine might still be inspected. Being outside the trigger proves neither absence of inspection nor absence of another inspection requirement.\\r\\n- **Universal requirement:** A certified fleet requires every vehicle to pass inspection. One failed vehicle proves the fleet is not certified. This combines quantifier negation with contraposition, so it belongs after Joshua\'s quantifier phase introduces those operations.\\r\\n- **Compound principle:** A valid submission requires both a signature and a date. Missing either establishes invalidity. Having both does not itself establish validity.\\r\\n- **Chain with uncertainty:** Enrollment guarantees account creation; account creation guarantees an identifier. Enrollment probably improves attendance. Enrollment therefore guarantees an identifier, while improved attendance remains uncertain.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Proposed LSAT U adaptation\\r\\n\\r\\nUse this as a model for advanced application practice after foundations, not as a beginner lesson order. Assign each original exercise to its specific skill and difficulty, while retaining a general mixed route. Replace live private guesses with a committed answer and reasoning prompt before feedback. Explain errors and supply a fresh transfer item. Offer timing separately at Medium and Advanced. These are design proposals, not features verified in the source.\\r\\nresearch-lsatlab-conditional-lesson.md\\r\\n# LSAT Lab conditional lesson: complete caption coverage\\r\\n\\r\\nResearch date: 2026-10-01. [Conditional Logic | LR](https://app.lsatlab.com/video-library/?videoid=16784), Patrick Tyrrell, published 2020-07-28. Observed Vimeo embed: 438082783. Parent verified player runtime 24:34. Caption source: `raw/sources/lsat-lab-lectures/16784/source.en-US.vtt`, native en-US track. No audio playback or board inspection is claimed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Source summary\\r\\n\\r\\nThe lesson begins with rule meaning and four possible fact positions, establishing valid triggering and invalid reversal/negation. Contraposition expands immediately to compound conditions. Chaining then contrasts rule conclusions with factual conclusions, including a partly satisfied compound trigger. Translation follows these operations: certainty, requirements, indicator direction, negative universals, exception language, and biconditionals. Training uses rhetorical inference questions, two explicit early pause tasks, equivalent translations, and a ten-item pause-and-solve worksheet with an indicator reference. The instructor reviews each item’s indicator, diagram direction, negation, and contrapositive. Later items demand interpretation beyond the memorized list and compound negation. The closing prioritizes indicator fluency, contraposition, compound negation, and avoiding invalid moves. Automated feedback, timed practice, mastery checks, and actual LSAT question IDs are absent from the captions. Quantifiers receive a brief translation aside, not a full treatment.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Chronological factual topic ledger\\r\\n\\r\\nTimes identify approximate teaching transitions in overlapping subtitle cues. Entries are topic labels and observed activity metadata.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Time | Topic | Observed training format |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| 00:10–00:31 | Objectives | Introduction |\\r\\n| 00:31–01:02 | Arrow; certainty; sufficient/necessary | Concrete rule |\\r\\n| 01:02–01:41 | Positive trigger; absent trigger | Contrasting cases |\\r\\n| 01:41–02:31 | Positive consequent; reversal; flaw | Contrast and warning |\\r\\n| 02:31–02:58 | Absent consequent | Inference question |\\r\\n| 02:58–04:05 | Contraposition; invalid negation | Explanation |\\r\\n| 04:05–04:37 | Compound antecedent; AND/OR negation | Symbolic demonstration |\\r\\n| 04:37–05:14 | Compound consequent contraposition | Explicit pause; worked answer |\\r\\n| 05:14–05:45 | Rule conclusion versus fact conclusion | Task distinction |\\r\\n| 05:45–06:37 | Three-rule chains; intermediate inferences | Worked symbolic chain |\\r\\n| 06:37–07:11 | Disjunctive outcome with eliminating fact | Worked symbolic inference |\\r\\n| 07:11–07:53 | Partly satisfied conjunction; residual conditional | Explicit pause; worked answer |\\r\\n| 07:53–09:05 | Certainty; universals; guarantees; requirements | Recognition and requirement rephrasing |\\r\\n| 09:05–09:29 | Equivalent wording | Pause to inspect slide examples |\\r\\n| 09:29–10:19 | Indicator columns; semantic categories | Reference list |\\r\\n| 10:19–11:45 | Negative universal | Plausibility contrast; alternate translations |\\r\\n| 11:45–12:53 | Negative quantifier rephrasing | Brief comparison |\\r\\n| 12:53–14:49 | Unless/until/without | Two equivalent approaches; simple examples |\\r\\n| 14:49–16:29 | Exception language with compounds | Parentheses; negation; alternate formulation |\\r\\n| 16:29–17:51 | Biconditional indicators | Two arrows versus same-status cases |\\r\\n| 17:51–18:48 | Otherwise; explicit opposite rule | Worked interpretation |\\r\\n| 18:48–19:29 | Ten-item worksheet instructions | Reference aid; pause; translation plus contraposition |\\r\\n| 19:29–19:49 | Item 1: when | Answer review |\\r\\n| 19:49–20:15 | Item 2: implies | Answer review |\\r\\n| 20:15–20:32 | Item 3: no | Answer review |\\r\\n| 20:32–20:49 | Item 4: each | Answer review |\\r\\n| 20:49–21:18 | Item 5: unless | Two approaches |\\r\\n| 21:18–21:53 | Item 6: never | Unlisted-word interpretation |\\r\\n| 21:53–22:19 | Item 7: any; alternative will reading | Scope and ambiguity |\\r\\n| 22:19–22:39 | Item 8: only | Answer review |\\r\\n| 22:39–23:18 | Item 9: without plus AND | Compound negation; alternate approach |\\r\\n| 23:18–23:42 | Item 10: prerequisite | Unlisted-word interpretation |\\r\\n| 23:42–24:20 | Fluency goals | Recap |\\r\\n| 24:20–24:35 | Outro | End material |\\r\\n\\r\\nNo proprietary worksheet sentences or answer bank are reproduced here.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original analysis: prerequisites and learning demand\\r\\n\\r\\nThis compact lesson assumes the learner can handle abstract letters and elementary negation almost immediately. It introduces AND/OR contraposition approximately four minutes in, before detailed indicator translation. That makes it useful as a compressed overview or refresher; a ground-up independent pathway would benefit from more isolated practice before the combined tasks. This judgment concerns instructional demand, not evidence of learner outcomes.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe four fact-position cases teach an important boundary: from S→N, S licenses N and ¬N licenses ¬S; ¬S and N alone leave the other term undetermined. Students must interpret uncertainty as an answer rather than feel compelled to infer something.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe linking section requires a different output type from triggering. Rules alone yield another relationship. Adding a fact can yield a factual consequence. A fact satisfying part of an AND antecedent can also simplify the remaining conditional demand. This last operation merits its own assignable skill in LSAT U rather than being hidden under general linking.\\r\\n\\r\\nTranslation strategy is partly syntactic and partly semantic. The reference identifies arrow placement, but unlisted words and equivalent requirement readings require understanding necessity. The lesson therefore does not justify teaching indicator memorization as sufficient mastery.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe practice sequence shifts from guided cases to a mixed worksheet and delayed instructor review. This is feedback through worked explanation after the student pauses. Captions provide no evidence of answer entry, immediate adaptive feedback, a scored diagnostic, retries with fresh items, or gating. A ten-item mixed worksheet is one observed training event, not a complete inventory of LSAT Lab exercises.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original LSAT U examples and assignable skills\\r\\n\\r\\nAll examples below are new and are not paraphrases of source exercises.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Fact positions:** every licensed pilot has passed an exam. Test separately what follows from licensed, not licensed, passed, and not passed.\\r\\n- **Compound contraposition:** inspected AND sealed → dispatchable. If not dispatchable, at least one prerequisite failed. Students must not infer both failed.\\r\\n- **Rule versus fact:** regional → registered; registered → approved. Derive regional → approved. Only after a named applicant is regional may the student derive that applicant’s approval.\\r\\n- **Residual condition:** code AND badge → entry; entry → attendance. Given the badge, code → attendance still remains conditional until a code fact is supplied.\\r\\n- **Equivalent exception translations:** equipment operates only when a safety check has passed. Require both a necessity reading and its contrapositive.\\r\\n- **Biconditional scope:** a display lights exactly when the circuit is active. Contrast an explicitly given two-way rule with an unsupported reversal of a one-way rule.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor Joshua\'s Beginner/Medium/Advanced model, start with a single operation, then mix operations, then vary language and compounds. Use a separate general mixed assignment at each level. These are design proposals, not LSAT Lab\'s observed level definitions.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Nuances and source-fidelity limits\\r\\n\\r\\nThe short negative-quantifier aside includes few, most, and not-all transformations. In LSAT U, define the intended mathematical meaning of few before equating it with most-not; everyday usage can be vague. No existence assumption should be silently imported into a universal rule. The captions do not give a full quantifier inference lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe certainty discussion includes guaranteed causal wording. LSAT U should distinguish the logical guarantee encoded by a sentence from proof of causation in an argument. The lesson\'s broad certainty framing is a recognition heuristic, not a complete account of every kind of statement.\\r\\n\\r\\nOtherwise creates a biconditional in the discussed case because the other branch supplies the opposite outcome. It should not be taught as automatically biconditional in every sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\nNative-track labeling does not establish transcription accuracy. Captions contain obvious substitutions involving contrapositive, flaw, letters, names, and ordinary nouns. One compound explanation labels the inferred side inconsistently; diagrams are necessary to verify its intended symbols. The item with alternative any/will readings requires the unseen sentence and subject scope to adjudicate fully. The slide\'s complete indicator list, displayed diagrams, and exact written worksheet were not recovered by reading captions. Do not fill these gaps from guesses.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Coverage check\\r\\n\\r\\nAll 573 numbered cues were read from opening to final cue; the initially truncated middle was read separately. First cue: 00:02.960. Final cue: 24:33.080–24:35.140. Only gaps greater than two seconds are the initial 2.960-second lead-in and 6.030 seconds before the final outro cue. Overlapping cues are normal here. Final timestamp exceeds the observed 24:34 runtime by 1.140 seconds; preserve this mismatch rather than trimming the source.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis establishes complete coverage of the supplied caption stream and its teaching sequence. It does not establish audiovisual fidelity, complete board content, or a complete LSAT Lab curriculum.\\r\\nresearch-lsatlab-core-class.md\\r\\n# Core class develops application through contrasted mistakes\\r\\n\\r\\nSource: [Conditional Logic](https://app.lsatlab.com/video-library/?videoid=32874), Matt Sherman, 2026-07-26. Parent verified Vimeo 1213147919, duration 87:18.68. All 1,398 automatic-caption cues inspected chronologically through 87:18.412. Audio/slides unverified; final student question cuts off.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Time | Teaching and training |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| 00:02–02:25 | Introduces precision and common application types; assumes a prior primer. |\\r\\n| 02:25–23:49 | Parallel flaw: independent attempt/poll, student explanation, conclusion identification, unless translation, reversal versus valid triggering/contraposition. Discusses when structural shortcuts work. |\\r\\n| 24:27–49:20 | SA: attempt/poll, map chain and conclusion, predict bridge, compare contraposed bridge with reversal, weak support and restatement. Repeated terms can signal rules without familiar indicators. |\\r\\n| 49:23–70:32 | Harder parallel flaw: distinguish negating a whole conditional from negating its terms; test counterexamples; require matching both flaw and structure. Briefly introduces nested-condition equivalence. |\\r\\n| 70:35–85:53 | Harder SA: locate novel conclusion term, distinguish useful bridge from existing implication, reject possibility as insufficient here, simplify compound conclusion before bridging. |\\r\\n| 85:57–87:18 | Recaps reversals/negations and indicator direction; unfinished question. |\\r\\n\\r\\nTraining cycles: independent attempt, poll, learner reasoning, teacher correction, contrasting answers. Prerequisites are repeatedly repaired. New demands include rule refutation and compound gaps. Four worked questions; no formal mastery gate observed. This application class is not a complete beginner sequence.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original examples, not provider exercises\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Unless:** A shipment cannot depart unless it is labeled. Departure → labeled. Labeled alone does not prove departure. An unlabeled shipment cannot depart.\\r\\n- **Missing bridge:** Delayed deliveries cause missed deadlines. Missed deadlines cause penalties. The argument concludes delayed deliveries lower supplier ratings. A bridge from penalties to lower ratings proves that conclusion; repeating that delays cause penalties adds no new bridge.\\r\\n- **Refuting a rule:** To disprove “Every registered vehicle is inspected,” find a registered vehicle that is not inspected. An inspected vehicle that is unregistered does not disprove that rule. Negating the rule means such a counterexample exists; it does not mean every registered vehicle is uninspected.\\r\\n- **Nested rule:** “If an application is complete, then if it is approved it receives funding” is equivalent to “Complete and approved → receives funding.” Neither condition alone suffices.\\r\\n- **Compound conclusion:** The premises already prove that a qualifying project is documented. The conclusion says a qualifying project is documented and audited. The missing bridge must establish auditing; it need not re-establish documentation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Proposed adaptation for LSAT U\\r\\n\\r\\nTurn each contrast into an individually assignable skill at Beginner, Medium and Advanced, then include the same skills in mixed practice. Preserve the committed first attempt and explanation before feedback. Follow correction with a fresh original item. Separate untimed understanding from optional Medium/Advanced timing. Treat selective diagramming as a choice supported by skill and task structure, rather than a universal speed rule.\\r\\nresearch-lsatlab-quantifiers.md\\r\\n# LSAT Lab quantifiers: complete caption review\\r\\n\\r\\nResearch date: 2026-10-01. [Quantifiers](https://app.lsatlab.com/video-library/?videoid=33015), Matt Sherman, 2026-08-27. Vimeo 1221968872; observed runtime 83:36.320. Caption source: `raw/sources/lsat-lab-lectures/33015/source.en-x-autogen.vtt`. Source-derived teaching summary and ledger below are deliberately concise. Later analysis and examples are original.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Teaching and training in presentation order\\r\\n\\r\\nThis class assumes conditional knowledge, introduces quantified language, develops combination patterns with counterexamples, then trains transfer through three polled questions and student explanations. Feedback addresses direction, answer strength, scope, and efficient diagramming. A student requests a separate translation worksheet; the instructor reports none available.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Interval | Teaching focus |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| 00:00–02:54 | All/most/some; ranges; direction; reversibility |\\r\\n| 02:54–06:56 | Indicators; not-all; few versus a few |\\r\\n| 06:56–10:48 | Plurality; language interpretation |\\r\\n| 11:03–16:58 | Some+some; some+most; three most+most configurations; countermodels |\\r\\n| 16:58–21:39 | Questions; concrete majority-overlap example |\\r\\n| 21:52–28:45 | Some+all; poll; common-term location |\\r\\n| 28:53–33:16 | Most+all; retained versus weakened quantifier |\\r\\n| 33:24–35:14 | All+all; pattern recap |\\r\\n| 35:17–50:07 | Application 1: negated categories; contraposition; pairwise inferences; answer elimination |\\r\\n| 50:07–52:11 | Worksheet request; next-question setup |\\r\\n| 52:11–67:55 | Application 2: mixed quantifiers; reversal; diagram overinterpretation; amounts; subject scope |\\r\\n| 67:59–81:45 | Application 3: selective diagramming; relevant majority pair; strength elimination |\\r\\n| 81:51–83:28 | Frequency guidance; closing |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original analysis: what LSAT U should learn from the design\\r\\n\\r\\nThe chronology supports Joshua\'s decision to place quantity after conditionals: the class relies on arrow direction, contraposition, common terms, and valid chains before adding quantified relationships. It does not separately remediate these prerequisites.\\r\\n\\r\\nTraining demand progresses from identifying a statement\'s strength to testing whether a proposed connection is forced. Numerical or spatial countermodels provide a reason for failure, rather than merely teaching a list of permitted patterns. Live polls expose disagreement; students then explain their reasoning while the teacher diagnoses it. This creates richer feedback than displaying the correct letter alone.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first application requires combining negative categories with a quantified existence statement. The second exposes errors in reversing strength, importing an unasserted region into a drawn set, comparing counts from percentages, and omitting the restrictive part of a subject. The third rewards reading the entire stimulus before drawing, because several relationships can be irrelevant to the required inference. These distinct demands should become independently assignable LSAT U skills, followed by mixed practice.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe observed worksheet request reveals a potential packaging gap in this class, not proof that the platform has no quantity activities. Independent learners need short translation and inference drills before complex question transfer, plus fresh feedback after an error. A class recording can demonstrate reasoning but does not itself supply that practice loop.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original accuracy checks before adaptation\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Most means greater than 50%, not a minimum of 51%.** A group can have 50.1% possessing a property. Use exact thresholds in teaching and assessment.\\r\\n- **Some means at least one, not at least 1%.** One member of a large group may be far below 1%. Keep counts and proportions distinct.\\r\\n- **All does not by itself assert existence in ordinary formal conditional reasoning.** From all A are B and all A are C, a B/C overlap requires an A to exist. The class\'s infer-down and shared-antecedent all/all explanations omit that premise. In its first application, a separate some statement establishes relevant existence; that can repair an inference in that context, but not the unconditional general rule.\\r\\n- **Most entails some; it is not equivalent to some.** A momentary equality-style caption should not become course wording.\\r\\n- **No new cross-term inference is not no inference of any kind.** Premises can still yield restatements, existential weakening, or reversals of some. Scope the pattern rules to their intended new endpoint connection.\\r\\n- **A some/most prohibition needs scope qualifications.** Nested subgroup statements can encode additional information. General pattern shortcuts assume the specific three-term arrangement under discussion; they must not override explicit subset structure or extra premises.\\r\\n- **Few and context-sensitive adverbs need careful semantics.** A platform\'s heuristic classification is not proof of a universal lexical equivalence. Teach the weakest warranted claim and distinguish plurality from majority.\\r\\n- **A drawing\'s blank region does not establish members.** Use marked witnesses or explicit cardinalities when proving overlap or building counterexamples.\\r\\n- Reported test-frequency guidance is the instructor\'s estimate, not a verified distribution of current tests.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original examples for our version\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Same denominator:** of 100 festival volunteers, 60 speak French and 60 speak Arabic. At least 20 speak both. Change the numbers to 51 and 51; the guaranteed intersection becomes much smaller. This trains why the output need not be most.\\r\\n2. **Different denominators:** most photographers are club members, and most club members are cyclists. Construct a larger club containing many cyclists outside the photographer group. This trains why apparent arrow alignment is insufficient.\\r\\n3. **Existence plus universal:** at least one archivist is bilingual; all bilingual archivists can translate the catalog. Identify a witness and carry that witness through the universal rule.\\r\\n4. **Universal without existence:** every purple badge holder is cleared and every purple badge holder is trained. An empty purple-badge group satisfies both. Add an explicit badge holder before concluding overlap exists.\\r\\n5. **Scope:** most night-shift nurses are certified. Keep night-shift in the quantified subject; do not diagram this as most nurses are certified.\\r\\n6. **Strength and quantities:** some river samples are contaminated and most lake samples are contaminated. Neither fact compares the number of contaminated samples without group sizes.\\r\\n\\r\\nBeginner work can isolate meaning, direction, and marked witnesses. Medium can combine a quantified statement with a universal and contrast valid with invalid pairs. Advanced can add negative terms, scope, redundant information, countermodels, and LSAT transfer. General mixed assignments and targeted assignments should coexist at all three levels; Medium and Advanced can optionally be timed.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Caption coverage and limitations\\r\\n\\r\\nAll 1,350 numbered cues were read chronologically through the final sign-off; the initial truncated middle was separately reread. First cue starts 00:02.880; final cue ends 83:28.255, leaving 8.065 seconds before the observed player endpoint. There are six gaps greater than 15 seconds: 22:24.828–22:49.228; 23:09.628–23:43.268; 35:49.596–38:43.786; 51:02.770–51:23.610; 52:11.270–55:16.080; 68:18.985–68:39.065. Context suggests poll setup and independent solving; audio silence is not independently verified. Some auto-cues themselves span long intervals with very little text, so gap detection alone cannot establish audio completeness.\\r\\n\\r\\nAutomatic captions confuse some with sum, omit visual referents, and include student mistakes that are subsequently corrected. No full audiovisual review, poll screenshot verification, or board capture was performed. No actual question IDs appear in the reviewed captions; none are inferred from topics. This establishes complete review of the available caption stream, not verbatim fidelity or complete coverage of LSAT Lab\'s quantifier curriculum.\\r\\nresearch-lsatlab-structure.md\\r\\n# LSAT Lab: verified organization and conditional teaching evidence\\r\\n\\r\\nUpdate 2026-10-01: the complete native en-US caption stream for Conditional Logic | LR (video 16784) has now been read. See [the chronological lesson analysis](research-lsatlab-conditional-lesson.md) for all teaching stages, the ten-item practice sequence, timing, learning demands, and fidelity limits. The browser limitation below describes the initial pass; it no longer means lesson content is wholly unexamined. Captions establish content coverage, while audio, boards, and interactive exercises remain unverified.\\r\\n\\r\\nAlso completed: [Quantifiers, video 33015](research-lsatlab-quantifiers.md), Matt Sherman, 2026-08-27. All 1,350 auto-caption cues reviewed; 83-minute class organized into quantified meaning, language, combination patterns, and three polled applications. The report records existence and threshold corrections required before adaptation. This supplements the earlier library metadata; it does not establish complete platform coverage.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The personalized Study Plan supplies a fuller training pathway\\r\\n\\r\\nThe parent research session subsequently inspected the signed-in personalized Study Plan. The table preserves its observed relevant card order. It is not a universal mandatory sequence. Time allocations are scheduled metadata; they do not establish actual time needed. Set IDs identify banks, not unique skills.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Order | Visible activity or set | Observed demand and allocation |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| 1 | Conditional Logic topic | 7h30 allocation; video; Level 1 Start; Levels 2–5 disabled; scheduled class Watch |\\r\\n| 2 | Conditional Logic main video | 30 scheduled minutes; actual player 24:34 |\\r\\n| 3 | Diagram Logic 1 | Flashcards; 10-minute allocation, 7-minute timer; difficulties 0–1 |\\r\\n| 4 | Easier 1, set 11 | 9 questions; levels 1–3; 42-minute process allocation |\\r\\n| 5 | Conditional Rephrase | AI activity spanning four indicator families; 10-minute allocation, 7-minute timer |\\r\\n| 6 | Easier 2, set 14 | 7 questions; levels 2–3; 12 minutes plus untimed review |\\r\\n| 7 | Conditional Inference Tuneup | Flashcards; 10-minute allocation, 7-minute timer |\\r\\n| 8 | Negations Practice | 7-minute allocation, 6-minute timer |\\r\\n| 9 | Negation Station | AI activity; 10-minute allocation |\\r\\n| 10 | Easier 3, set 17 | 7 questions; levels 1–2; 12 minutes |\\r\\n| 11 | Easier 4, set 21 | 9 questions; levels 1–2; 12 minutes |\\r\\n| 12 | Medium 1, set 44 | 10 questions; levels 2–4; 15 minutes |\\r\\n| 13 | Medium 2, set 89 | 7 questions; untimed; mostly sufficient assumption and principle |\\r\\n| 14 | Conditional Diagramming Level 3 | Explicit passing criterion: 4 of last 5 correct |\\r\\n| 15 | Medium 6, set 92 | 8 questions; 14 minutes |\\r\\n| 16 | Quantifiers Medium 2, set 97 | 7 questions; untimed; tests 65–70 |\\r\\n| 17 | Medium 3, set 124 | 7 questions; average difficulty 4; 12 minutes; appears on two schedule cards |\\r\\n| 18 | Medium 4, set 49 | 9 questions; 15 minutes |\\r\\n| 19 | Harder 1, set 147 | 8 questions; 16 minutes |\\r\\n| 20 | Harder 2, set 126 | 7 questions; 12 minutes |\\r\\n| 21 | Harder 3, set 133 | 6 questions; level 5; 11 minutes |\\r\\n| 22 | Harder 4, set 9 | 7 questions; process activity |\\r\\n\\r\\nSource: signed-in LSAT Lab Study Plan, inspected by the parent research session. The topic\'s five displayed levels are stronger evidence of staged skill training than the video library\'s regular/advanced class labels. Disabled levels establish visible structure only; their tasks, prerequisites, and unlocking behavior were not inspected. The specific Level 3 card establishes its own 4-of-5 criterion, not every activity\'s passing rule.\\r\\n\\r\\nOriginal design implication: distinguish concept instruction, symbolic flashcards, language rephrasing, inference rehearsal, general negation, and authentic question application. Difficulty and timing operate across these formats. Mixed question sets develop transfer but do not replace specific-skill remediation. Two cards using set 124 are repeated scheduling of the same bank; do not count them as fresh independent assessments. The personalized plan interleaves one quantified set; Joshua\'s LSAT U design instead places the full quantified phase after conditionals, while preserving separate assignments.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Corrections required before adapting observed teaching\\r\\n\\r\\nThe parent identified three accuracy hazards in subsequently inspected activities. These are original logical checks, not source quotations:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Negating more than half means **at most half**, including exactly 50%; restricting the negation to 49% is incorrect.\\r\\n- A normative conclusion about what should be done need not be the consequent in every conditional. Separate deontic content from arrow direction rather than impose a universal normative-right/empirical-left shortcut.\\r\\n- Naming a complementary category is not a general negation method. The complement must cover every possibility excluded by the original claim; scope, compounds, and quantifiers still require their own treatment.\\r\\n\\r\\nPreserve these issues as explicit adaptation checks. Familiar source authority does not make an oversimplified rule suitable for LSAT U.\\r\\n\\r\\nResearch date: 2026-09-30. Source access: signed-in Codex browser. This is an original analysis, not a transcript or copied exercise bank.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What was inspected live\\r\\n\\r\\n[Video Library](https://app.lsatlab.com/video-library/) has separate Lessons and Recordings views. Lessons groups Logical Reasoning by teaching purpose. The observed order is: broad argument understanding; famous reasoning flaws; common reasoning patterns; Inference Family; Assumption/Objection Family; Match Family; Paradox. This is displayed topic order, not proof of mandatory prerequisites.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe common-pattern group contains Rebuttals, Causation, **Conditional Logic**, and Comparison. It provides a broad conditional lesson rather than a visibly separate lesson for each indicator group. The visible Lessons view did not expose a dedicated quantifier course or a series of micro conditional exercises. That does not establish that none exist elsewhere.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Exact visible source | Teacher | Published date | Verified role |\\r\\n|---|---|---|---|\\r\\n| [Conditional Logic \\\\| LR](https://app.lsatlab.com/video-library/?videoid=16784) | Patrick Tyrrell | 2020-07-28 | Lesson; described as an introduction to conditional reasoning and its LR role |\\r\\n| Must Be True \\\\| LR | Matt Sherman | 2021-01-07 | Inference Family lesson |\\r\\n| Necessary Assumption \\\\| LR | Matt Sherman | 2020-01-14 | Assumption/Objection Family lesson |\\r\\n| Sufficient Assumption \\\\| LR | Matt Sherman | 2020-01-14 | Assumption/Objection Family lesson |\\r\\n| Principle \\\\| LR | Matt Sherman | 2018-12-27 | Assumption/Objection Family lesson |\\r\\n| Parallel Flaw \\\\| LR | Matt Sherman | 2021-03-11 | Match Family lesson |\\r\\n| Parallel \\\\| LR | Patrick Tyrrell | 2020-05-22 | Match Family lesson |\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly the Conditional Logic detail URL was inspected. Other titles and metadata were observed on the Lessons listing; their contents were not viewed.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe initial Recordings listing also showed recurring Conditional Logic, Quantifiers, Must Be True, and Sufficient Assumption classes, including separately titled advanced classes. Relevant examples: Conditional Logic (Matt Sherman, 2026-07-26); Conditional Logic (adv) (Patrick Tyrrell, 2026-07-15); Quantifiers (Matt Sherman, 2026-08-27); Must Be True (Patrick Tyrrell, 2026-08-27). Dates identify recordings, not curriculum stages. Regular/advanced titles support differentiated instruction; they do not establish Joshua\'s requested three-level system.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What an existing archived lesson demonstrates\\r\\n\\r\\n[Must Be True, video 33013](https://app.lsatlab.com/video-library/?videoid=33013), Patrick Tyrrell, 2026-08-27, 97 minutes. Evidence comes from the existing local archive and its coverage analysis, not fresh playback. Summary: the opening separates contraposition, connecting rules, and applying a fact. It contrasts valid bridges with rules that share only a result, uses contraposition to reveal hidden links, addresses illegal reversal and negation, and distinguishes guaranteed consequences from frequency claims. Five worked LSAT applications explore requirements, compounds, subject scope, passive wording, and answer strength. Diagramming is presented as useful when it resolves complexity. This establishes substantive conditional transfer within an inference lesson, not a complete standalone conditional curriculum.\\r\\n\\r\\nArchive: `corpus/lectures/logical-reasoning/must-be-true/core/2026-08-27-33013/`. The source-caption archive is complete; full audio fidelity remains unverified. Adaptation corrections are recorded separately in its coverage ledger.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Teaching progression we can infer, with limits\\r\\n\\r\\nThe library places conditional reasoning among reusable argument patterns, then organizes applications by question family. The archived MBT class demonstrates movement from explicit operations to worked LSAT applications. A useful LSAT U progression is therefore meaning and translation → valid transformations → rule linking versus fact-triggering → application. This is an LSAT U design inference, not a verified timestamp-by-timestamp outline of LSAT Lab\'s Conditional Logic lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\nTraining evidence is strongest for instructor explanations, contrasting valid/invalid moves, repetition as a fluency goal, and worked LSAT questions. Number of repetitions, student answer interface, automated feedback, difficulty progression, mastery gates, and independent reassessment were not verified in this pass. A video library is not itself evidence of a complete independently guided pathway.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Original LSAT U practice proposals\\r\\n\\r\\nUse one shared rule set to isolate different operations: every certified guide is insured; every insured guide has a permit.\\r\\n\\r\\n- Translate each rule before combining them.\\r\\n- Derive certified → permit without assuming any certified guide exists.\\r\\n- Add the fact that Mira is certified; derive Mira\'s insurance and permit.\\r\\n- Add instead that Mira lacks a permit; use contraposition to infer she is not certified.\\r\\n- Ask whether two rules ending in insured can be connected; require explanation of why a shared destination supplies no bridge.\\r\\n\\r\\nThese are original example proposals. Beginner work can isolate one operation; Medium can require choosing the operation; Advanced can vary language and compound structure. Timing remains optional for Medium and Advanced. Quantifiers belong in the following phase under Joshua\'s requirement, with their own assignable skills.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Unverified portion and browser limitation\\r\\n\\r\\nThe Conditional Logic detail page exposed a Vimeo player iframe, but player controls were unavailable through the inspected DOM. Subsequent navigation and state reads timed out. No full lesson playback, drill completion, transcript extraction, answer submission, or progress change was intentionally performed. Duration and actual fine-grained lesson content remain unverified. The temporary research tab was closed successfully after these failures.\\r\\n\\r\\nNext useful inspection: the Conditional Logic lesson\'s visible chapters/captions if available; a current advanced conditional recording; a Quantifiers recording; and Study Plan practice links. Capture concise teaching summaries and exercise roles, without copying a complete lesson or question bank.\\r\\n"}'}]

question-level review | One operation / select operation / dense mixed evidence |\n+| Sufficient bridge | Locate gap, insert assumption, rerun proof; distinguish restatement | Reuse Missing Link/SA bootcamp; separately teach illustrative generalization | Guided pools; gap verified complete sequence | Explicit rule / compound trigger / distinguish task types |\n+| Quantified meaning and direction | Identify range, denominator and witness; explain reversibility limits | Legacy Some/Most notes; gap reviewed targeted bank | Some/all / most / vague language and scope |\n+| Quantified negation and linking | Build countermodels; carry witnesses through valid rules | Legacy notes; gap full progression | One negation / valid pairs / mixed negative terms |\n+| General mixed practice | Choose procedure across learned skills; feedback names operation missed | Reuse General/hub/guided drills; unified routing needed | Isolated operations mixed / combined operations / advanced transfer |\n+\n+For new formats, start with paper-first production and a deterministic reveal/self-comparison, matching the existing interaction model. Proposed additions include allowed-case cards, counterexample construction and error diagnosis. Automatic grading of those new interactions would require implementation and validation; no superiority or existing availability is claimed. A drill can be assigned without requiring the student to repeat the teaching sequence.\n+\n+### Original Group 1 miniunit: learning what an if-clause guarantees\n+\n+**Teach.** A sufficient condition is enough to establish the result in this rule. It need not be the only route. In an ordinary conditional statement, the complete if-clause goes before the arrow. Clause order in the sentence does not determine arrow direction.\n+\n+**Worked example.** “If a parcel receives express service, it receives tracking.” Define E as express service and T as tracking. Write E→T. An express parcel must have tracking. A tracked parcel need not be express. Tracking could accompany another service. The forbidden case is E together with not T.\n+\n+**Guided practice.** “A visitor receives an entry code if the visitor registers online.” First identify the if-clause: registers online. Then identify the guaranteed result: entry code. Write R→C. Explain why C→R would add a guarantee the sentence never supplied. Reveal these steps after the student attempts them.\n+\n+**Independent practice.** Translate “If an exhibit is temporarily closed, its tickets remain valid.” Then answer separately what follows from a closed exhibit, and from valid tickets. Answer: closed→valid; closure establishes validity, while validity alone leaves closure unknown. Ask for a plain-language explanation before reveal.\n+\n+**Error repair.** If the student reverses the rule, return to the two complete clauses and ask which fact the sentence guarantees a result from. If they infer that an open exhibit has invalid tickets, construct the allowed case of an open exhibit with valid tickets. Repair direction and unsupported inference separately.\n+\n+**Fresh transfer.** “A refund is issued whenever a canceled reservation was prepaid.” Treat canceled-and-prepaid as the complete sufficient condition: (canceled AND prepaid)→refund. A prepaid reservation alone is insufficient. This is a Medium extension once AND prerequisites are taught, not a surprise Beginner requirement.\n+\n+Advanced Group 1 work would add embedded modifiers and distractor rules while preserving the same operation. The separately assignable drill draws fresh items from the appropriate level; the sequence includes explanation and repair. Exact item counts, timing defaults and advancement criteria remain for Joshua to decide.\n*** End Patch"));

Willingham\nL7: \nL8: January 7, 2013\nL9: \nL10: Tags:\nL11: \nL12:   * \ue200cite\ue2022†Academia\ue201 L13:   * \ue200cite\ue2023†Education\ue201 L14:   * \ue200cite\ue2024†Learning\ue201 L15:   * \ue200cite\ue2025†Students\ue201 L16:   * \ue200cite\ue2026†Teaching\ue201 L17: \nL18: \ue200cite\ue2027†Log in to Save for Later†member.psychologicalscience.org\ue201 L19: \nL20: \ue200cite\ue2028†Image: Close-up photograph of a perfect grade on a scantron test.\ue201 L21: Read the Full Text (\ue200cite\ue2029†PDF†psi.sagepub.com\ue201 , \ue200cite\ue20210†HTML†psi.sagepub.com\ue201 )\nL22: Some students seem to breeze through their school years, whereas others struggle, putting them at risk for getting lost in our educational system and not reaching their full potential. Parents and teachers want to help students succeed, but there is little guidance on which learning techniques are the most effective for improving educational outcomes. This leads students to implement studying strategies that are often ineffective, resulting in minimal gains in performance.\nL23: What then are the best strategies to help struggling students learn?\nL24: Fortunately for students, parents, and teachers, psychological scientists have developed and evaluated the effectiveness of a wide range of learning techniques meant to enhance academic performance. In this report, Dunlosky (Kent State University), Rawson (Kent State University), Marsh (Duke University), Nathan (University of Wisconsin–Madison), and Willingham (University of Virginia) review the effectiveness of 10 commonly used learning techniques.\nL25: The authors describe each learning technique in detail and discuss the conditions under which each technique is most successful. They also describe the students (age, ability level, etc.) for whom each technique is most useful, the materials needed to utilize each technique, and the specific skills each technique promotes. To allow readers to easily identify which methods are the most effective, the authors rate the techniques as having high, medium, or low utility for improving student learning.\nL26: Which learning techniques made the grade? According to the authors, some commonly used techniques, such as underlining, rereading material, and using mnemonic devices, were found to be of surprisingly low utility. These techniques were difficult to implement properly and often resulted in inconsistent gains in student performance.\nL27: Other learning techniques such as taking practice tests and spreading study sessions out over time — known as distributed practice — were found to be of high utility because they benefited students of many different ages and ability levels and enhanced performance in many different areas.\nL28: The real-world guidance provided by this report is based on psychological science, making it an especially valuable tool for students, parents, and teachers who wish to promote effective learning. Although there are many reasons why students struggle in school, these learning techniques, when used properly, should help provide meaningful gains in classroom performance, achievement test scores, and many other tasks students will encounter across their lifespan.\nL29: About the Authors (\ue200cite\ue20211†PDF†psi.sagepub.com\ue201 , \ue200cite\ue20212†HTML†psi.sagepub.com\ue201 )\nL30: ## Editorial: Applying Cognitive Psychology to Education: Translational Educational Science\nL31: \nL32: By Henry L. text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/curriculum-analysis.md\n@@\n-| Practical inference orientation | Attempt a small inference; revisit after teaching; explain the evidence | Reuse MBT teaching; build brief orientation | One rule / choose relevant rule / distractors |\n+| Practical inference orientation | Follow a concrete worked inference first; try a similar guided case; explain the evidence | Reuse MBT teaching; build brief orientation | One rule / choose relevant rule / distractors |\n@@\n-| MBT/MSS application | Prove guaranteed result or identify support strength required | Reuse hub/guided drills/lecture; question-level review | One operation / select operation / dense mixed evidence |\n+| MBT/MSS application | Distinguish demands: MBT proves a guarantee; MSS selects strongest warranted support, which need not be certain | Reuse hub/guided drills/lecture; question-level review | One operation / select operation / dense mixed evidence |\n@@\n For new formats, start with paper-first production and a deterministic reveal/self-comparison, matching the existing interaction model. Proposed additions include allowed-case cards, counterexample construction and error diagnosis. Automatic grading of those new interactions would require implementation and validation; no superiority or existing availability is claimed. A drill can be assigned without requiring the student to repeat the teaching sequence.\n+\n+Alternating worked examples with student attempts, asking students to retrieve taught operations before reveal, and returning to them after a delay have a research basis. The [IES practice guide](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/1) recommends worked-example/problem alternation, spaced learning and retrieval through quizzes. The [Dunlosky learning-techniques review](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/journals/pspi/learning-techniques.html) rates practice testing and distributed practice highly across varied learning contexts. These sources support those design choices; they do not establish that this LSAT curriculum is superior or determine our exact review intervals.\n+\n+Prerequisite safeguards: teach basic negation before Groups 3–4; teach AND/OR before compound tasks within any group; teach whole-claim negation before rule-refutation tasks; and teach quantified existence before quantified applications. The later quantifier phase supplies the witness where an overlap inference needs one. Universal rules alone do not establish members. A contrapositive preserves the rule, while negating the whole rule asserts a counterexample. Group labels identify our translation taxonomy, not distinct laws of logic: Group 3 exception wording and Group 4 exclusions can have equivalent negative representations.\n*** End Patch"));

## assistant

Intro to LR supplies a useful **course shell**, but it is currently a specific course implementation rather than a configurable bootcamp engine.

- **Main sequence:** 13 ordered actions: eight lesson notes, three native labs, and two official-question practice sets. The path interleaves teaching and practice. [introToLrPath.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/content/introToLrPath.ts:34)
- **Supporting modules:** reference tools, flashcards, indicator reference, simulator, hard-sentence lessons/capstone, diagnostics, SRS, journal, and settings. These sit outside the 13-action main sequence. The workbook route presently redirects to lessons. [routes.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/routes.tsx:120)
- **Native practice:** Main Conclusion Lab has 20 questions; First Sentence vs. Rebuttal Lab has 20; Conclusion Type Lab has 12. Their interactions are tailored to those skills. [introDrills.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/modules/drills/introDrills.ts)
- **Official practice:** two fixed six-question pools launch through Guided Drills, resume saved sessions, and record course completion. The launcher explicitly recognizes Intro’s source string. [GuidedDrillStart.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/pages/GuidedDrillStart.tsx:317), [Drill.tsx](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/pages/Drill.tsx:2721)

**What can carry over:** the workspace layout, lesson/practice navigation pattern, path rail, next-step hero, preparation/run/review shells, reference layout, saved-session mechanisms, and diagnostics presentation. Their visual components are reusable; embedded Intro routes, identifiers, and content require parameterization.

**What Conditional needs added:**

1. A Conditional course namespace for progress, routes, completion IDs, and practice pools. Current progress IDs are user-based without a course namespace, so directly copying the hook risks sharing Intro progress. [useModuleProgress.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/hooks/useModuleProgress.ts)
2. Separately addressable skill units and beginner/medium/advanced variants. Current teacher assignment supports a whole activity, guided drill, or bootcamp topic; guided drills support level/count overrides, but bootcamp assignments do not select a skill or difficulty. [assignWork.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/lib/assignWork.ts:16)
3. Conditional-specific practice interactions and feedback. The existing labs cannot teach translation, contrapositives, compound rules, or missing links unchanged.
4. A general practice-to-course bridge. Intro’s fixed pool/source handling is hardcoded; Conditional needs its own registered pools and return/completion handling.
5. Explicit links to reusable Activities. Existing activity assignment snapshots the whole activity. The inspected bootcamp path uses native labs and official guided practice, rather than a general Activity-backed unit system.

Signed-in persistence already uses local-first Supabase synchronization through `bootcamp_kv`; anonymous persistence uses local storage/IndexedDB. This infrastructure can carry over with distinct course records. [factory.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/persistence/factory.ts)

One discrepancy: Simulator’s hint describes completing three labs, but `unlockNext` currently unlocks it after Conclusion Type Lab alone. Avoid copying this as a verified prerequisite rule. [ordering.ts](C:/Users/Joshu/dev/lsatu-connected-experience/src/bootcamps/main-conclusion/lib/ordering.ts)

Read-only inspection completed. No app changes, publication, or tests performed.

This is the canonical voice doc: route all student-facing and brand copy through it. Built from a grill with Joshua (2026-06-13), then tested and enriched against the full corpus of his real correspondence (944 messages he authored, mid-2025 to mid-2026, from the Gmail takeout; 2026-07-18). Claims below marked with a quote are evidenced by that corpus.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt replaces the old two-register / 15-named-tools \\"preserve verbatim\\" profile (deleted 2026-06-10) and folds in the brand/marketing register the earlier draft was missing.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core voice (every register)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe constant under all three registers below. This is Joshua on the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Quiet authority.** State the value and let it land. Never oversell, never beg, never perform enthusiasm.\\r\\n- **Specific, never generic.** Real scores, the actual skill, the student\'s own history. Praise is a specific observation, not \\"great job.\\"\\r\\n- **Honest about the work, gentle about the person.** Be blunt that the LSAT is hard (\\"expect this to be exhausting and very challenging\\"). Never be blunt about a student\'s shortcomings. Honesty points at the material; warmth points at the person. When someone slips, nudge gently, never accuse.\\r\\n- **Light, grounded metaphor, understated in email.** In his real correspondence the recurring image is quiet: \\"partner with you on your LSAT journey,\\" \\"getting set up,\\" \\"foundational.\\" The vivid images (runway, climb, march toward November, an easy door to walk through) belong to authored teaching and brand copy, not to email. Keep metaphor light and grounded; never float off into abstraction.\\r\\n- **Balanced rhythm.** Short declaratives plus one slightly longer warm beat. Air between ideas. Each idea gets its own line. Real messages are short and single-purpose (median ~280 characters).\\r\\n- **Plain professional diction.** No corporate jargon, no startup hype (\\"unlock,\\" \\"crush,\\" \\"level up,\\" \\"game-changer\\" — \\"crush\\" appears once in 944 messages). Contractions are the norm, not the exception. Exclamation points are genuine, not performed: a warm message often carries one, occasionally more, especially in openers (\\"Sorry for such a long delay!\\"). He is not exclamation-averse.\\r\\n- **Forward-looking.** End on the next step or what\'s ahead.\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** Use periods, colons before lists, the middot (·) as a separator, and numbered steps for procedures.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Openings, closings, and signature phrases\\r\\n\\r\\nThe mechanical fingerprint of his email, from the real corpus. Match these when drafting as Joshua.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Greeting.** \\"Hi [Name],\\" is the default (used ~519x). \\"Hey [Name],\\" for established/returning students (~229x, warmer). \\"Hello [Name],\\" (~105x) and \\"Dear [Name],\\" (~18x, formal) for first contact or a more formal note.\\r\\n- **Sign-off.** \\"Best,\\" and \\"Best regards,\\" are the workhorses (~360x / ~237x). \\"Thanks,\\" when it\'s a favor or logistics (~146x). \\"Warmly,\\" / \\"Warm regards,\\" (~54x) for a genuinely warm note. \\"Talk soon,\\" (~9x) for someone he\'ll see again soon.\\r\\n- **Signature.** Almost always signed **\\"Joshua\\"** (844 of 944 messages). The name is near-universal; include it.\\r\\n- **Signature phrases (his verbal fingerprint, use naturally, don\'t overuse):** \\"let me know\\" (by far the most common, ~390x), \\"looking forward,\\" \\"I hope\\" / \\"hope all is well\\" / \\"hope you,\\" \\"no worries at all,\\" \\"happy to\\" / \\"more than happy to,\\" \\"just wanted to make sure,\\" \\"make sure,\\" \\"no rush,\\" \\"of course.\\"\\r\\n- **Punctuation he actually uses:** semicolons (correctly, ~41x); ellipses essentially never. (For em-dashes, the hard rule in Core voice governs — never.)\\r\\n\\r\\n## The apology / accountability move\\r\\n\\r\\nOne of his most frequent and characteristic behaviors, and worth naming on its own. When he is late to reply, or missed or mishandled something, he opens by owning it plainly, often with a brief honest reason, then pivots straight to the fix. No over-apologizing, no excuses dressed up.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'m so sorry. I thought I had let you know ... I clearly didn\'t communicate that as well as I should have.\\r\\n\\r\\n> I\'ve been away from work for personal reasons, but I\'m back now and getting caught up.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pattern: own it in the first line, give the real reason in one clause, move to what happens next. Warm, candid, brief.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When something on his side broke (approved shape, 2026-09-11)\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the Sandra booking-error reply, edited by Joshua line by line over three drafts and then sent as-is. Use this shape whenever a student hit a bug or a mistake that was his. The sent text is the reference:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Hi Sandra,\\r\\n>\\r\\n> I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet. The page was showing a few times that the system then refused, and it looks like you landed on those. That is fixed now.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Your link is the same one as before:\\r\\n> [link]\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Pick any time it shows and it will book. If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Once again, my apologies.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Best,\\r\\n> Joshua\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Apology first, as the opening line.** \\"I\'m sorry about this. The error was on my end, not yours.\\" The ownership sits in the first two sentences, before any explanation.\\r\\n2. **State their position plainly, as a confirmation.** \\"To confirm: none of your bookings went through, so nothing is on the calendar yet.\\" Answer the question they actually asked. Don\'t mention the package or credits unless the situation calls for it.\\r\\n3. **One-sentence explanation, then \\"That is fixed now.\\"** No mechanics, no system names.\\r\\n4. **Hand them the next step, plus the manual fallback.** The link, \\"pick any time it shows and it will book,\\" and the offer to do it by hand: \\"If it\'s easier, just send me the time you were trying for and I\'ll add it to the schedule myself.\\"\\r\\n5. **Invite the next report:** \\"If you run into any other issues, let me know.\\"\\r\\n6. **Close with \\"Once again, my apologies.\\"** then \\"Best,\\" and \\"Joshua\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nCut from the draft, do not reuse:\\r\\n- \\"Sorry for the runaround\\" as a sign-off. The apology opens the email; it is not a closing quip.\\r\\n- \\"You will get a calendar invite with the Google Meet link right after.\\" Do not narrate what the system will send; it reads as a promise about machinery.\\r\\n- \\"You have all 10 sessions\\" / \\"nothing was used from your package.\\" Leave the package out unless it is needed; the reassurance they want is that nothing is booked, not an accounting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Situational micro-templates\\r\\n"}'}]

What follows?', 'L has a badge and does not work alone.', 'L must be a morning volunteer too.', 'Nobody with a badge works alone.', 'L first qualifies for the badge rule and then for the restricted no-working-alone rule.', 'Carry the evening-volunteer domain into the second trigger.'],\n+      ['All historical maps donated by residents are catalogued. Every catalogued map in the west room is scanned. Map W is historical and donated by a resident. Is scanning guaranteed?', 'No; being in the west room is missing.', 'Yes; catalogued means west-room.', 'No; historical maps cannot be scanned.', 'The first rule establishes cataloguing. The second needs both cataloguing and west-room location.', 'Find the qualifier that the first result does not supply.'],\n+      ['Every approved permit expires in June. Every permit that expired in June last year was renewed. Permit T is approved this year. Is renewal established?', 'No. The expiry facts refer to different years.', 'Yes. June expiry always implies renewal.', 'T was renewed last year.', 'This year’s approval produces this year’s June expiry, not last year’s expiry.', 'Do not merge dates because the month matches.'],\n+      ['No certified trial boats lack radios. Every radio-equipped passenger boat is inspected. Boat V is a certified trial boat. What follows?', 'V has a radio; inspection needs passenger-boat status.', 'V is inspected automatically.', 'V lacks a radio.', 'Certified trial status guarantees a radio. The inspection rule also requires passenger-boat membership, which is not supplied.', 'Keep boat type inside both complete triggers.'],\n+    ],\n+  }),\n*** End Patch"));

Closed denies both routes.', 'Contrapose the entire OR-trigger direction.'],\n+      ['A ↔ B. B ↔ (C AND D). C is true and D false. Missing D rules out B, and A requires B.', 'Use the necessary side before chaining back to A.'],\n+    ],\n+  }),\n+  unit({ id: 'whole-rule-negation', title: 'Deny the rule with a counterexample', area: 'complex', phase: 'conditional',\n+    prerequisites: ['domain', 'de-morgan', 'biconditionals'], goal: 'Distinguish the denial of a universal conditional from its equivalent contrapositive.',\n+    teaching: ['To deny “Every permitted vehicle is inspected,” find at least one permitted vehicle that is not inspected. For a compound rule, satisfy its entire trigger and deny its entire result. Keep the original population and time restrictions.'],\n+    method: ['Write the original trigger and result.', 'Construct a case with the trigger true.', 'Make the required result false, respecting its scope.', 'State at least one such case rather than a new universal rule.'],\n+    workedExample: { statements: ['Claim: Every licensed stall displays its permit.'], reasoning: ['Licensed → displays permit.', 'A violating stall must be licensed and fail to display the permit.'], conclusion: 'At least one licensed stall does not display its permit denies the claim.' },\n+    commonMistake: { mistake: 'Offering the contrapositive as the negation.', repair: 'An equivalent rule cannot contradict the original. Show an actual trigger-without-result case.' },\n+    guided: ['Deny “Every approved file is signed and dated.”', 'Some approved file is unsigned or undated.', 'Every unsigned file is unapproved.', 'No approved file is signed.', 'The trigger must hold while the joint result fails. One missing required component is enough.', 'Negate the whole AND result inside a counterexample.'],\n+    practice: [\n+      ['Negate “All sculptors are patient.”', 'Some sculptor is not patient.', 'No sculptor is patient.', 'All impatient people are nonsculptors.', 'One sculptor without patience refutes the universal rule. it is equivalent.', 'Yes; both sides are negative.', 'Yes; the arrow is reversed.', 'Reversing and negating both sides preserves the original rule.', 'Compare the cases each rule excludes.'],\n+      ['Negate “All evening buses stop at Pine or Oak.”', 'Some evening bus stops at neither Pine nor Oak.', 'Some morning bus skips Pine.', 'Some evening bus skips Pine but stops at Oak.', 'The counterexample retains evening-bus status and fails both OR alternatives.', 'Deny the entire alternative result.'],\n+      ['Negate “All signed and witnessed forms are valid.”', 'Some signed, witnessed form is invalid.', 'Some signed form is invalid, whether witnessed or not.', 'Every invalid form is unsigned.', 'The counterexample needs the complete joint trigger, not merely signing.', 'Satisfy every AND-trigger component.'],\n+      ['“Not all vouchers expire in June.” What is guaranteed?', 'At least one voucher does not expire in June.', 'Every voucher expires outside June.', 'Most vouchers do not expire in June.', 'The denial requires one exception, not a majority or universal absence.', 'How many exceptions are needed to defeat all?'],\n+      ['Negate “Every coastal clinic with a generator stays open and accepts transfers.”', 'Some coastal clinic with a generator is closed or refuses transfers.', 'Some inland clinic with a generator is closed.', 'All coastal clinics refuse transfers.', 'Retain both coastal status and generator possession, then deny at least one required result.', 'Preserve the domain and negate the compound consequent.'],\n+      ['Negate “Each accredited institute offers a seminar or a workshop.”', 'At least one accredited institute offers neither.', 'At least one accredited institute offers no seminar but a workshop.', 'No workshop provider is unaccredited.', 'Neither alternative may hold in a counterexample. A workshop alone satisfies the original OR.', 'One surviving alternative prevents the counterexample.'],\n+      ['Deny “A pass is active iff its fee is paid.”', 'Some pass is active but unpaid, or paid but inactive.', 'Some pass is inactive and unpaid.', 'Every inactive pass is unpaid.', 'A biconditional contains two rules. Either direction can fail; matching false statuses does not violate it.', 'Look for a mismatch between the two statuses.'],\n+    ],\n+  }),\n+  unit({ id: 'mbt', title: 'Draw only conclusions the facts force', area: 'application', phase: 'conditional',\n+    prerequisites: ['triggering', 'de-morgan', 'domain'], goal: 'Use conditional rules for guaranteed inference without treating support as certainty.',\n+    teaching: ['A Must Be True task asks what cannot be false if the premises hold. Start with a worked chain: every approved report is logged; every logged report is stored; R is approved. R must be stored.', 'Most Strongly Supported asks for the strongest available support, which can be weaker than certainty. Do not import that lower standard into MBT. Conversely, a guaranteed conclusion can be appropriate in an MSS task when the facts establish it. Match the actual question demand.'],\n+    method: ['Accept the stated premises for the task.', 'Track valid arrows, contrapositives and facts.', 'Predict a guaranteed result when possible.', 'Reject choices requiring reversal, missing facts or stronger quantities.'],\n+    workedExample: { statements: ['All registered boats have radios.', 'All radio-equipped boats can signal.', 'Boat N is registered.'], reasoning: ['Registered → radio → can signal.', 'N supplies the initial trigger.'], conclusion: 'N can signal.' },\n+    commonMistake: { mistake: 'Choosing a plausible answer that could still be false.', repair: 'Try to construct a world where all premises hold and the answer fails. If one exists, the answer is not forced.' },\n+    guided: ['All poets are readers. All readers are curious. Which must be true?', 'All poets are curious.', 'All curious people are poets.', 'Some poets exist.', 'The forward chain yields poets → curious. It supplies neither reversal nor existence.', 'Draw the chain without adding a member.'],\n+    practice: [\n+      ['Every cleared parcel is stamped. K is cleared. What must be true?', 'K is stamped.', 'Every stamped parcel is cleared.', 'K is the only cleared parcel.', 'The fact directly fires the rule.', 'Start with the established cleared fact.'],\n+      ['All blue keys open gate A. Key R does not open gate A. What must be true?', 'R is not blue.', 'R is blue.', 'No key opens gate A.', 'The missing required result rules out the trigger for R alone.', 'Use the contrapositive for this key.'],\n+      ['All archivists are careful. Which is forced?', 'Any careless person is not an archivist.', 'At least one archivist exists.', 'All careful people are archivists.', 'The contrapositive follows; existence and reversal do not.', 'Find the equivalent rule, not an added fact.'],\n+      ['All audited files are signed or sealed. F is audited and unsealed. What must be true?', 'F is signed.', 'F is unaudited.', 'F is both signed and sealed.', 'Auditing requires at least one result; unsealed excludes the second.', 'Narrow the OR result using the supplied negative fact.'],\n+      ['(Training AND insurance) → authorization. Authorization → badge. Lea has training and insurance. What must be true?', 'Lea has a badge.', 'Every badged person has insurance.', 'Training alone guarantees a badge.', 'Both trigger components establish authorization, which establishes a badge.', 'Keep the joint trigger intact before chaining.'],\n+      ['A café’s sales increased after a sign changed. The facts give no rule linking signs to sales. Which standard is appropriate for an MBT causal conclusion?', 'A cause is not guaranteed by that sequence alone.', 'The sign must have caused the increase.', 'Any plausible explanation is automatically MBT.', 'Temporal sequence alone allows other explanations. Strong support and certainty are different demands.', 'Could the sales change have another explanation while the facts remain true?'],\n+      ['Every coastal depot with a crane is inspected. Inspection → record. Depot D is coastal and has no record. What must be true?', 'D lacks a crane.', 'D is inland.', 'D is inspected.', 'No record gives not inspected. Since coastal is established, a crane would create the forbidden joint trigger.', 'Use the failed result and the known half of the trigger.'],\n+      ['Some gardeners are cooks. Every cook is trained. Which is guaranteed?', 'Some gardeners are trained.', 'All gardeners are trained.', 'Most trained people are cooks.', 'The existing gardener-cook witness carries through the universal cook rule. It does not cover all gardeners.', 'Carry the same existing witness through the arrow.'],\n+      ['Every member who submits an essay qualifies. Every qualifying member gets a badge or a voucher. Member V submits an essay and gets no badge. What is forced?', 'V gets a voucher.', 'Every voucher holder qualifies.', 'V gets neither benefit.', 'The restricted joint trigger is satisfied. Qualification gives alternatives; no badge leaves voucher.', 'Retain member status at each step.'],\n+    ],\n+  }),\n+  unit({ id: 'sufficient-assumption', title: 'Build a bridge that guarantees the conclusion', area: 'application', phase: 'conditional',\n+    prerequisites: ['mbt', 'direct-linking', 'no-link', 'and-or'], goal: 'Supply a premise that makes the argument valid, including gaps inside a chain.',\n+    teaching: ['In a sufficient-assumption task, the conclusion is given and the bridge is missing. “All trained guides are certified; Jo is trained; therefore Jo is listed” becomes valid if all certified guides are listed. Add the candidate, then prove the conclusion.', 'The bridge can connect the last premise to the conclusion or join two earlier facts. A broader rule can still suffice. A sufficient answer need not be the only possible bridge, and it need not be necessary. Merely increasing likelihood does not meet the guarantee demand.'],\n+    method: ['Separate premises from the conclusion.', 'Identify the exact disconnected predicates.', 'Add one candidate as a new premise.', 'Prove the conclusion from the expanded set.'],\n+    workedExample: { statements: ['Every repaired bike is inspected.', 'Bike M is repaired.', 'Conclusion: M is safe.'], reasoning: ['We have repaired → inspected and repaired(M).', 'Add inspected → safe.', 'Repaired(M) now yields inspected(M), then safe(M).'], conclusion: 'Every inspected bike is safe is sufficient.' },\n+    commonMistake: { mistake: 'Choosing a bridge in the wrong direction.', repair: 'Start from what the premises establish. Which addition suffices?', 'All assigned ushers have badges.', 'All badge holders are assigned.', 'Some assigned ushers have badges.', 'Assigned(Eli) becomes badge(Eli) under the first rule.', 'What new arrow starts with assigned?'],\n+      ['P is a gardener. Conclusion: P is patient. Which addition suffices?', 'Every gardener is patient.', 'Every patient person is a gardener.', 'Some gardeners are patient.', 'The universal forward rule applies directly to P.', 'A some statement need not include P.'],\n+      ['A → B. Which addition suffices?', 'C → D.', 'D → C.', 'D → A.', 'The new rule extends the forward chain to D.', 'Finish the chain in the conclusion’s direction.'],\n+      ['All restored maps are catalogued. Which addition suffices?', 'Every insured account is audited.', 'Every audited account is insured.', 'Every uninsured account lacks records.', 'Insured → audited → records contraposes to no records → uninsured.', 'Build a rule whose contrapositive reaches the negative conclusion.'],\n+      ['R is trained and insured. Which addition suffices?', 'Anyone trained and insured is eligible.', 'Every eligible person is trained.', 'Some trained people are eligible.', 'R satisfies both components of the added joint trigger.', 'Check the entire trigger, including insurance.'],\n+      ['Every applicant with a portfolio is interviewed. Sufficiency does not require the narrowest or necessary bridge.', 'Test whether the added statement actually guarantees V’s conclusion.'],\n     ],\n   }),\n+  unit({ id: 'necessary-assumption', title: 'Find what the argument cannot do without', area: 'application', phase: 'conditional',\n+    prerequisites: ['sufficient-assumption', 'whole-rule-negation'], goal: 'Separate a required assumption from a powerful but optional sufficient bridge.',\n+    teaching: ['A necessary assumption is something the argument needs. It need not prove the conclusion by itself. If the argument concludes that Jo can enter using a ticket rule, it must assume that the rule applies to Jo’s ticket. A rule admitting everyone could guarantee entry but is not required.', 'Negate a candidate precisely and ask whether the argument can still establish its stated conclusion. “All” is denied by one exception, not by “none.” Conditional necessary assumptions can be narrow compatibility claims. Do not choose a universal bridge merely because it would fix the argument.'],\n+    method: ['Identify the argument’s route to its conclusion.', 'Ask what that route requires.', 'Negate the proposed assumption accurately.', 'Check whether the negation defeats that route, rather than merely weakening it a little.'],\n+    workedExample: { statements: ['Only registered entrants may compete.', 'The author concludes that Mara may compete because she has a pass.'], reasoning: ['May compete → registered.', 'For the author’s conclusion to hold, Mara must be registered.', 'If Mara is not registered, the conclusion violates the stated requirement.'], conclusion: 'Mara is registered is necessary, though registration alone does not guarantee permission.' },\n+    commonMistake: { mistake: 'Selecting a broad sufficient rule as though the argument needs that entire rule.', repair: 'Negate the broad rule with one exception. If the argument’s subject can still qualify, the rule was not necessary.' },\n+    guided: ['Only insured drivers may use the rental car. The author concludes that Theo may use it. What is required?', 'Theo is insured.', 'Every insured driver may use it.', 'Every driver is insured.', 'The conclusion requires insurance for Theo; neither universal statement is required.', 'Apply the stated necessary condition to the conclusion’s subject.'],\n+    practice: [\n+      ['Only members can vote. Which negation tests that assumption?', 'No usher is trained.', 'Not every usher is trained.', 'Some ushers are trained.', 'The denial of at least one is none. The author concludes that project R may proceed and is funded. What is necessary?', 'P has a captain.', 'All teams with captains compete.', 'P has both a captain and a manager.', 'Competition requires at least one role. With no manager, captain is the remaining required option.', 'Narrow the required OR using the stated negative fact.'],\n+      ['Jo is a poet. The author concludes that Jo is patient. Is “All poets are patient” necessarily required?', 'No; the conclusion could hold for Jo while another poet is impatient.', 'Yes; it is the only sufficient statement.', 'No; Jo must be impatient.', 'The broad bridge is sufficient but its negation can be an exception involving someone else. Jo’s conclusion can still hold.', 'Try a counterexample outside the argument’s subject.'],\n+      ['Every restored building must be insured and inspected. The author concludes that building B is restored, using evidence about its age. What is required?', 'B is insured and inspected.', 'Every old building is restored.', 'Every inspected building is old.', 'The restored conclusion entails both necessary conditions. They are required but do not guarantee restoration.', 'Keep both components of the necessary AND result.'],\n+      ['Only projects with a permit and an access plan may start. The argument concludes that R may start. Which negation would directly defeat a required assumption?', 'R lacks a permit or lacks an access plan.', 'R has both.', 'Some other project lacks a permit.', 'The conclusion requires both conditions for R. Failure of either contradicts permission to start.', 'Negate the whole joint requirement for the same project.'],\n+      ['All award recipients must attend or appoint a representative. The author concludes that N receives the award, and says N will not attend. Which is necessary but not by itself sufficient?', 'N appoints a representative.', 'Every representative receives an award.', 'Everyone receives an award.', 'An award for an absent N requires a representative. Having one alone does not prove an award.', 'Distinguish a remaining requirement from a guarantee of the award.'],\n+    ],\n+  }),\n+  unit({ id: 'flaw', title: 'Explain the invalid move', area: 'application', phase: 'conditional',\n+    prerequisites: ['mbt', 'whole-rule-negation'], goal: 'Identify an unsupported conditional inference and explain it with a counterexample.',\n+    teaching: ['From A → B and B, concluding A affirms the necessary condition. B could occur without A. From A → B and not A, concluding not B denies the sufficient condition. Which assessment is correct?', 'The inference is valid.', 'It affirms the necessary condition.', 'It denies the sufficient condition.', 'Not certified → not listed is the contrapositive.', 'Reverse and negate both sides to compare.'],\n+      ['(License AND insurance) → entry. R has a license. Therefore R may enter. What is the flaw?', 'The member could receive only a discount.', 'OR requires both benefits.', 'A member cannot have a locker.', 'The rule guarantees at least one benefit, not this particular one.', 'Can the alternative result satisfy the rule?'],\n+      ['All evening volunteers are trained. What is the flaw?', 'The author reverses the chain from its final result.', 'The author validly chains the premises.', 'The premises imply V lacks a radio.', 'Rescue → inspected → radio does not give radio → rescue.
